title: Medium vs. Substack vs. Kahana: Where Should Your Writing Live?
excerpt: Medium fits a standalone article. Substack fits an ongoing publication and subscriber list. Kahana fits when the useful unit is a collection people can return to together.
defaultImageQuery: three reading desks in a warm library, articles notes and a shared shelf
seoTitle: Medium vs Substack vs Kahana | Where Writing Should Live
metaDescription: Compare Medium, Substack, and Kahana for discovery, subscribers, and collections. Medium for articles, Substack for a publication, Kahana for a hub readers can return to.
content:
Medium, Substack, and Kahana start a reader in different places. The useful question is what you want them to open, and come back to.

While exploring these platforms, I kept coming back to how easily a reader can begin. On the Medium entry path I visited, sign-in and signup prompts felt more prominent than the opportunity to browse first. That was my experience of that route, rather than a test of every way to read a Medium article. Substack stood out for a different reason: Notes creates room for short conversations between longer publications, giving writers another place to exchange ideas and hear from readers. Reviewing Kahana’s documented workflow brought a third question into focus: what happens when your work includes several pieces that people should be able to return to together?

These differences matter more than a broad claim that one platform is best. This comparison combines those browsing observations with official documentation to consider discovery, reader contact, paid access, and the practical shape of a writer’s work.

Quick verdict

  • Choose Medium if your main product is an article and you want to participate in an existing reading network. Its distribution mechanisms and Partner Program can be relevant even before you have built a large following, subject to eligibility. They do not guarantee readers or income.
  • Choose Substack if you want an ongoing publication with email subscribers, recurring paid subscriptions, and conversation between editions. Its export tools are especially relevant when keeping a portable subscriber relationship matters.
  • Consider Kahana if the useful unit is a collection: a writing guide with worksheets, a research library, a workshop recording with notes, or an archive with supporting material. A hub gives those pieces a shared destination with optional paid access.

Medium: publish an article within a reading network

Medium is relevant when the article itself is the main experience. A reader opens a story, follows its argument, and may continue to another writer or publication.

My initial browsing experience felt oriented toward joining the platform. It would be too broad to say that Medium never permits exploration before signup. Its own distribution guidance identifies direct links and external search as routes through which readers can find stories. A homepage prompt, an account requirement, and a paid story’s paywall are different forms of friction. Test the route your readers will actually use before making a universal claim.

Medium’s distribution documentation describes opportunities through its network, publication followers, and search indexing. These are potential paths to discovery. Publishing an article does not mean every member, or every person interested in its subject, will encounter it.

For paying readers, Medium offers a consistent membership experience across authors. Its membership guide lists unlimited ad-free story access, text-to-speech, offline lists in the mobile apps, access to its Mastodon instance, and custom domains for profiles or publications. The plans page also lists creating publications. These benefits cover different jobs: audio and offline access serve readers, while domains and publications support writers.

The earning proposition needs similar precision. Medium’s current Partner Program eligibility includes an active membership, at least one published story, a complete profile, supported payout eligibility, and an age requirement. A follower minimum is not listed there. Its enrollment guide describes earnings based on member engagement. Being eligible without an established audience is different from earning without readers.

SEO is part of the picture, but a platform’s search presence is not your personal ranking guarantee. Medium’s SEO explanation describes measures intended to support substantive writing and discourage spam. Choose Medium for a relevant readership and a suitable article format. Evaluate search traffic through results rather than assumptions about domain size.

Substack: publish regularly and stay in contact

Substack is a practical candidate when readers subscribe because they want the next piece from a particular writer. A recurring publication gives you a reason to return to their inbox, rather than relying entirely on another discovery session.

It also has a social layer. In my exploration, Notes felt familiar to X: short updates and exchanges alongside longer work. Substack’s Notes guide confirms that writers can share short posts and ideas across its network. Notes do not send as individual newsletter emails, although roundups or push notifications may surface them.

That creates a useful distinction. Your longer publication can explain an idea in depth. A Note can invite a response, share a question, or continue the conversation. Whether those exchanges produce useful feedback depends on the people participating. Having a reply feature does not establish the quality or activity of a community.

Substack’s feature guide documents publishing, email, discovery, comments, and Chat in one system. This offers more than an email delivery tool, but writers should still decide which activities they can maintain. A frequent social presence can become another commitment alongside preparing the publication itself.

Kahana: give related work a shared destination

A Kahana hub is a collection of files, folders, notes, and embeds. A hub starts private. Its creator can later share it by link or list it in the public Library. Monetization is a separate choice.

Consider a writer teaching character development. The work might include an explanatory article, a worksheet, annotated examples, and a recorded session. A hub can organize that package so readers have somewhere to return. This is an example workflow, not a tested customer result.

Library search covers hubs, authors, and communities, including most public non-adult listings for guests. Full Library browsing can be limited on small phones. A clear desktop collection is not enough if your audience mainly uses phones.

Communities are groups organized around reading, shared items, and conversation, with private and listed options. That can support discussion around a collection. This review did not test whether a particular genre has an active reader community there.

Kahana is worth evaluating when your readers need several related pieces together. For a writer whose main requirement is recurring email delivery, Substack addresses that job more directly. This review did not find a native creator newsletter or a complete mailing-list export on Kahana.

Kahana plan details: Pricing and When to upgrade. Medium and Substack publish their own fee pages and change them. Check those pages rather than treating this table as a permanent quote.

Migration and using platforms together

Before moving an archive, test a small representative sample. Check images, links, formatting, access settings, and how a reader gets to the next useful item. Preserve original files and document which links need updating.

Substack documents importing from other platforms, with steps that depend on the source. This review did not test a migration. Kahana’s current path is to organize the material yourself, with selected import and embed options. There is no one-click Medium or Substack migration.

A combined workflow may be simpler than replacing everything. Publish a recurring essay through your preferred publication, and link to a Kahana hub for worksheets or recordings. Alternatively, use Medium for selected standalone articles while maintaining a separate, consented subscriber relationship. Give readers a reason for each destination and keep the number of steps manageable.

Which should you choose?

Start with the work you want someone to read or use. If it is a standalone essay, evaluate Medium’s reading and distribution model. If the promise is an ongoing publication, evaluate Substack’s subscriber workflow. If the value sits in a connected collection, evaluate Kahana’s hubs.

Then ask what you can demonstrate: can a new reader find a relevant piece, understand the offer, and return to it? Discovery tools create possibilities, but reader growth and paid demand still need evidence.

For a resource collection, explore Kahana’s Library and consider whether one small hub would help your readers. Start with useful material you have rights to share and test the experience before moving an entire archive.
